## Overview

Working with GAMs and models containing penalised spline terms within the 'tidyverse' can be tedious and even difficult without a good understanding of these models themselves and how the model is returned by *mgcv* or other packages, and what the model objects contain. *gratia* is designed to help with
this.

*gratia* provides *ggplot*-based graphics and utility functions for working with
generalized additive models (GAMs) fitted using the *mgcv* package, via a
reimplementation of the `plot()` method for GAMs that *mgcv* provides, as well
as *tidyverse* compatible representations of estimated smooths. Additionally,
*gratia* supports several related packages that allow *mgcv*'s smooths to be
included in their models:

- *GJRM*,
- *glmmTMB*,
- *gamm4*,
- *scam*,
- *sdmTMB*

## Citation

If you use *gratia* in your work, please cite the package using:

Simpson, G. L., (2024). gratia: An R package for exploring generalized additive
models. *Journal of Open Source Software*, **9**(104), 6962,
<https://doi.org/10.21105/joss.06962>

## Features

```{r draw-gam-figure, fig.height = 6, fig.width = 9, echo = FALSE, fig.show = "hide", message = FALSE}
df1 <- data_sim("eg1", n = 400, seed = 42)
m1 <- gam(y ~ s(x0) + s(x1) + s(x2) + s(x3), data = df1, method = "REML")
draw(m1, residuals = TRUE, rug = FALSE)
```

```{r draw-gam-figure-2d, fig.height = 6, fig.width = 9, echo = FALSE, fig.show = "hide", message = FALSE}
df2 <- data_sim("eg2", n = 1000, seed = 42)
m2 <- gam(y ~ s(x, z), data = df2, method = "REML")
draw(m2)
```

```{r conditional-differences-figure, fig.height = 4, fig.width = 9, echo = FALSE, fig.show = "hide", message = FALSE}
df_groups <- data_sim("eg4", n = 400, seed = 42)
m_groups <- gam(y ~ fac + s(x2, by = fac) + s(x0),
  data = df_groups, method = "REML")
group_differences <- conditional_differences(m_groups, by = "fac",
  condition = list("x2", fac = c("1", "2")))
draw(group_differences, ylab = "Difference (group 1 - group 2)") +
  ggplot2::facet_null()
```

```{r derivatives-figure, fig.height = 4, fig.width = 9, echo = FALSE, fig.show = "hide", message = FALSE}
deriv <- derivatives(m1, select = "s(x2)", type = "central",
  interval = "simultaneous", seed = 42)
draw(deriv)
```

```{r appraise-figure, fig.height = 6, fig.width = 9, echo = FALSE, fig.show = "hide", message = FALSE}
appraise(m1)
```

```{r response-moments-figure, fig.height = 4, fig.width = 9, echo = FALSE, fig.show = "hide", message = FALSE}
data("mcycle", package = "MASS")
m_distribution <- gam(
  list(accel ~ s(times, k = 20), ~ s(times, k = 6)),
  data = mcycle, family = gaulss(), method = "REML")
response_moments <- conditional_moments(m_distribution, condition = "times",
  moments = c("mean", "sd"))
moment_plots <- draw(response_moments, xlab = "Time after impact (ms)")
moment_plots[[1]] <- moment_plots[[1]] +
  ggplot2::labs(y = "Mean acceleration (g)")
moment_plots[[2]] <- moment_plots[[2]] +
  ggplot2::labs(y = "Standard deviation (g)")
moment_plots
```

```{r smooth-samples-figure, fig.height = 4, fig.width = 9, echo = FALSE, fig.show = "hide", message = FALSE}
samples <- smooth_samples(m1, select = "s(x2)", n_draws = 20, seed = 42)
draw(samples)
```

* **Visualise model effects.** Plot smooths, parametric effects and interactions
  with `draw()`, including surfaces and effects that vary between groups.
  Customise individual plots or complete figures using native ggplot2 themes.
  For example, draw the smooths and partial residuals from a GAM:

  ![Estimated smooths and partial residuals from a GAM](man/figures/README-draw-gam-figure-1.png)

  Or plot a smooth surface:

  ![Estimated smooth surface from a GAM](man/figures/README-draw-gam-figure-2d-1.png)

* **Understand how effects and predictions change.** Estimate derivatives,
  compare smooths, contrast fitted responses between groups, and calculate
  accumulated local effects. Work with transformed covariates while displaying
  effects on their original scales. Here, `conditional_differences()` compares
  fitted responses for two groups across a covariate:

  ![Difference in fitted responses between two groups](man/figures/README-conditional-differences-figure-1.png)

* **Quantify uncertainty across smooths.** Calculate pointwise and simultaneous
  intervals for smooths, derivatives, differences and predictions. For example,
  estimate how quickly a smooth changes with `derivatives()` and draw its
  derivative with a 95% simultaneous interval:

  ![Derivative of a smooth with a simultaneous interval](man/figures/README-derivatives-figure-1.png)

* **Check models with diagnostics suited to their response distributions.**
  Use `appraise()` for an overview of model fit, or draw individual diagnostic
  plots. Check a wide range of response distributions, including categorical
  and censored responses, using appropriate residuals and posterior predictive
  checks. Plots designed for large datasets keep diagnostic displays readable
  while using all observations.

  ![Residual diagnostics for a GAM](man/figures/README-appraise-figure-1.png)

* **Explore the fitted response distribution.** Estimate and plot response
  means, variances and other distribution summaries, with uncertainty. These
  tools also work with models where several distribution parameters depend on
  covariates. Here, `conditional_moments()` shows how mean acceleration and its
  standard deviation vary with time in the motorcycle impact data:

  ![Estimated mean and standard deviation of acceleration over time](man/figures/README-response-moments-figure-1.png)

* **Simulate from fitted models.** Generate coefficient, smooth, derivative,
  fitted-response and predictive draws from approximate posterior
  distributions. Multiple chains, sampling diagnostics, and integration with
  [posterior](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=posterior),
  [coda](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=coda) and
  [bayesplot](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=bayesplot) support more
  extensive posterior exploration.
  For example, `smooth_samples()` generates possible smooth curves:

  ![Twenty draws of a smooth from its approximate posterior distribution](man/figures/README-smooth-samples-figure-1.png)

* **Use familiar tools across more model classes.** Explore shape-constrained
  models from [scam](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=scam) and
  `mgcv::scasm()`, as well as models from
  [GJRM](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=GJRM),
  [gamm4](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=gamm4),
  [glmmTMB](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=glmmTMB) and
  [sdmTMB](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=sdmTMB). See the articles on
  [SCAM](https://gavinsimpson.github.io/gratia/articles/scam-support.html),
  [glmmTMB](https://gavinsimpson.github.io/gratia/articles/glmmTMB-support.html)
  and [sdmTMB](https://gavinsimpson.github.io/gratia/articles/sdmTMB-support.html)
  for the operations supported by these model classes.


## Installing *gratia*

*gratia* is now available on CRAN, and can be installed with

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("gratia")
```

however *gratia* is under active development and you may wish to install the
development version from github. The easiest way to do this is via the binary packages of the development version that are provided by rOpenSci's R Universe service:

```{r install-r-universe, eval = FALSE}
# Install gratia in R
install.packages(
  "gratia",
  repos = c(
    "https://gavinsimpson.r-universe.dev",
    "https://cloud.r-project.org"
  )
)
```

Alternatively, install from source using the `install_github()` function from package *remotes*. Make sure you have *remotes* installed, then run

```{r install-github, eval = FALSE}
remotes::install_github("gavinsimpson/gratia")
```

to install the package.

## History

*gratia* grew out of an earlier package, *schoenberg*, itself a development of
the earlier package *tsgam*, which was originally intended to be used with GAMs
fitted to time series. As I was developing *tsgam* however it became clear that
the package could be used more generally and that the name "tsgam" was no longer
appropriate. To avoid breaking blog posts I had written using *tsgam* I decided
to copy the git repo and all the history to a new repo for the package under the
name *schoenberg*. At a later date someone released another package called
*schoenberg* to CRAN, so that scuppered that idea. Now I'm calling the package
*gratia*. Hopefully I won't have to change it again&hellip;

## Why *gratia*?

In naming his *greta* package, Nick
Golding observed the recent phenomena of naming statistical modelling software,
such as Stan or Edward, after individuals that played a prominent role in the
development of the field. This lead Nick to name his Tensor Flow-based package
*greta* after *Grete Hermann*.

In the same spirit, *gratia* is named in recognition of the contributions of
[Grace Wahba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grace_Wahba), who did pioneering
work on the penalised spline models that are at the foundation of the way GAMs
are estimated in *mgcv*. I wanted to name the package *grace*, to explicitly
recognise Grace's contributions, but unfortunately there was already a package
named *Grace* on CRAN. So I looked elsewhere for inspiration.

The English word "grace" derives from the Latin *gratia*, meaning "favour, charm,
thanks" ([according to Merriam Webster](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/grace)).

The chair that Grace Wahba currently holds is named after
[Isaac J Schoenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Jacob_Schoenberg), a
former University Madison-Wisconsin Professor of Mathematics, who in a 1946
paper provided the first mathematical reference to "splines". (Hence the
previous name for the package.)
